subject: math

objective.text: Draw a bar graph to represent a given data set.

explanations.title: Title, labels and scale first
explanations.text: Write the title first. Label the categories. Write the number scale. Then fill in the bars to match the table.

explanations.title: Horizontal and vertical bar graphs
explanations.text: A horizontal graph goes across and the scale is at the bottom. A vertical graph goes up and down and the scale is at the side. We compare how long or how tall the bars are.

explanations.title: The scale starts at 0
explanations.text: Like a ruler, the scale starts at 0. The space from 0 to the first line is a count of 1. We can turn the scale to go up like a ruler for height.

explanations.title: Comparison questions
explanations.text: To find how many more or fewer, compare the bars. You can subtract the two numbers.

source_ref.section: Student Debrief (what operation did you use?)

explanations.title: What a box stands for
explanations.text: So far each box or picture stands for one thing. It does not always have to be one.

examples.title: Our Birthdays
examples.text: The categories are seasons: fall, winter, spring and summer. Each bar shows how many students have a birthday in that season.

examples.title: Alicia's bugs
examples.text: Butterflies 5, spiders 14, bees 12 and grasshoppers 7. Each box on the scale equals one bug.

Scale starts at 0 and counts by ones

visual_generation_rules: Diffusion cannot count reliably. Any picture where an exact number of objects matters must be built by code (SVG or widget) or drawn by an artist.
Diffusion is allowed only for: style or background art, and single icons (one ball, one pencil, one leaf, one character) that code then tiles to the exact count.
Every visual must be checked by a person: the count shown must equal the stimulus in the question and the rubric answer key.
Animations are described as frames with exact counts per frame, so they can be built or generated and then checked frame by frame.
